The Tammar wallaby Macropus eugenii is a small macropodid marsupial endemic to southern and western Australia, and its life history has been studied extensively in both wild and captive populations. At parturition, the altricial neonate emerges after a remarkably brief gestation, and at birth the joey possesses a head length of only 0.6 cm [Lb = 0.6 cm], a diminutive dimension that reflects the extremely altricial state typical of marsupials. The wet weight at birth correspondingly registers a mere 0.370 g [Wwb = 0.370 g], making the newborn one of the smallest mammalian neonates relative to adult mass. This diminutive young then makes its way to the pouch, where it attaches to a teat for an extended period of dependent development. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of the species' resting physiology, which centre on a core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the female's gestation period has been measured at 28 days [tg = 28 days].

The pouch young of the Tammar wallaby undergoes a protracted period of growth and differentiation before it becomes nutritionally independent from its mother. Data derived from longitudinal head-length measurements indicate that the young attain a head length at weaning of 8 cm , a value that marks the transition to a diet of solid forage. At this same developmental milestone, the weaned juvenile typically reaches a wet weight of 1580 g [Wwx = 1580 g], representing a substantial fraction of the adult mass but still well below the ultimate size. The time since birth at weaning has been documented at 255 days since birth [tx = 255 days since birth], a period that aligns with the range of 245 to 270 days reported for permanent pouch exit in this species at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This prolonged period of lactation dependency is energetically costly for the female, and metabolic measurements conducted on non-reproducing individuals at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] have quantified the average yearly milk production at an estimated rate of approximately 28493.15 J per day .

As the growing individual continues its development beyond weaning, it eventually reaches the stage of sexual maturation, which in the Tammar wallaby is accompanied by notable increases in both skeletal dimensions and body mass. Measured head length at puberty, based on growth-curve data, averages 8.8 cm [Lp = 8.8 cm], while the wet weight at puberty is recorded at 2700 g [Wwp = 2700 g], indicating that roughly half of the ultimate adult mass is achieved by this point. Under the stable thermal conditions of captivity at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the time since birth at puberty averages approximately 335.5 days since birth [tp = approximately 335.5 days since birth], which equates to roughly 11 months, a value consistent with the species' relatively rapid maturation for a macropodid of its size. Ultimate head length for fully grown adults has been determined from the same dataset to be 9.1 cm [Li = 9.1 cm].

The fully grown adult Tammar wallaby exhibits a maximum recorded body mass, or ultimate wet weight, of 5000 g [Wwi = 5000 g], a value typical of a three-year-old individual according to captive records, though some variation exists among subspecies and populations. This adult size, while modest among macropodids, is associated with a striking reproductive physiology: females are capable of producing a single offspring per year, which translates to a maximum reproductive rate of one joey per 365 days [Ri = one joey per 365 days] when maintained at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This annual single-pouch-young strategy, combined with the capacity for embryonic diapause, allows the species to maintain a stable population trajectory even in the face of seasonal resource fluctuations. Longevity records for Macropus eugenii indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5510 days [am = approximately 5510 days] under captive conditions at the same thermoneutral temperature at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C].

Energetic studies on non-reproducing adult Tammar wallabies weighing approximately 4.3 kg have provided detailed accounting of daily energy fluxes under thermoneutral conditions at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. The daily food intake for a 4.3 kg individual amounts to 1,915,000 J per day , while the corresponding assimilation rate has been estimated at 1,133,000 J per day , reflecting the digestive efficiency typical of a herbivorous foregut-fermenting mammal at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. The inefficiency of this digestive process is evident in the faeces production rate, which has been calculated at approximately 516,592 J per day  for a 4.3 kg animal at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. These metabolic parameters collectively illustrate the energetic economy of a medium-sized macropodid that has evolved to thrive in the nutrient-poor, mediterranean-climate scrublands of its native range, where dietary quality and water availability impose tight constraints on daily energy balance.
